assessment: Illinois Extension lists 1 cup butter -> 3/4 cup oil for baking; by weight that is about 72-75 percent because butter is only about 80 percent fat (USDA FDC). Support covers fat uses; oil cannot cream with sugar so binding/creaming contexts are unsuitable.

Muffin trials replaced 25-100 percent of butter with avocado puree without significant physical differences (S5; S14); Wyoming Extension suggests 1 cup pureed avocado for 1 cup butter in brownies and chocolate bakes (S7); butter-cake trials show reduced volume and harder crumb because avocado does not cream (S6). The 1.0 ratio is convention and unsupported for creaming contexts.

Canned coconut milk is far higher in fat (23.8 g/100g vs about 1 g/100g for 1 percent milk in the bundled USDA-derived catalog) so the swap changes richness; supported as culinary convention for curries and sauces; no validated universal ratio found.
Illinois Extension lists tofu among plant proteins but no source gives a cheese-to-tofu substitution ratio; the 1.2 crumble ratio and the ricotta/feta mimic claim are unsupported.
Extension guidance covers yogurt-for-sour-cream but not yogurt-to-coconut milk; thickness differs and coconut products lack yogurt acidity and cultured proteins; the 0.9 ratio is unsupported.
Illinois Extension: 1 cup yogurt for 1 cup sour cream; thick plain or Greek yogurt gives a closer texture. Works in dips; sauces; and baking; and as a topping.
Blended avocado as creamy richness is culinary convention; no primary source for a 0.8 ratio (Wyoming guidance covers butter only).
Extension lists tofu as a plant protein to replace part or all of fresh meat; no measured ratio; protein density differs sharply (31 vs 8 g/100g in the bundled USDA-derived catalog).
Beans and other plant proteins are supported as meat replacements by extension guidance; the 1.3 ratio is convention; chickpeas add carbohydrate and fiber and deliver far less protein per weight.
Iowa State Extension states beans can substitute for meat in chili and tacos - exactly the bundled recipe contexts; the 1.2 ratio itself is convention.
Extension supports tofu as a meat substitute generally; no measured ground-meat ratio was found.

column14: No primary source found for a salmon-to-tofu substitution; the nori-for-a-seafood-hint claim is convention.
Mashed-chickpea 'tuna' salad is culinary convention; no primary source found for the swap or the 1.2 ratio.

assessment: Illinois Extension supports zucchini noodles as a pasta alternative; the 1.5 weight ratio is convention and zoodles are not nutritionally one-for-one (USDA FDC composition).

column14: The service note claims cubed sweet potato adds body to sauces; no primary source found.
Toasted sweet-potato rounds as bread is culinary convention; no primary source found.
Lettuce wraps are culinary convention; no primary source found; lettuce is a lower-energy carrier not an equivalent replacement (USDA FDC composition).
Lettuce leaves for tortillas is culinary convention; no primary source found.
Rice as a porridge base for oats is culinary convention; no primary source found.

assessment: Extensions support 1/4 cup (about 60 g) mashed ripe banana per large egg (about 50 g) - a ratio near 1.2 by weight; production ships 0.6 and under-doses by about half. Support is for binder/moisture in moist baked goods (cakes; muffins; pancakes); banana does not aerate; coagulate; or leaven like egg and is unsuitable where egg is the main protein.

Bundled USDA-derived sugars: honey 82.1 g/100g vs banana 12.2 g/100g; at a 1.5 weight ratio the swap delivers about one fifth of the sugar so sweetness equivalence is unsupported; the note itself says adjust to taste.
Peer-reviewed assay: citric acid 1.44 g/oz lemon vs 1.38 g/oz lime - interchangeable for acidity at 1:1; aroma differs.
Same assay supports the reverse swap; flavor (not acid chemistry) is the difference.

column14: Scallions are milder than bulb onions as culinary wisdom but no quantitative pungency (pyruvate) comparison was found; the 0.7 ratio is unsupported; the late-addition advice applies to green tops.
No quantitative pungency data found; the 1.4 ratio is unsupported; white scallion bases are closer to onion than the green tops.
Similar cooking method is convention; composition differs (USDA FDC); no substitution source found.
Riced broccoli for rice is culinary convention; no primary source found; large energy and starch gap (USDA FDC).
